nodes.label: The two Davids
nodes.full: After Rusudan's death in 1245 the Mongol great khan Güyük confirmed in 1247 two claimants, David VII Ulu, son of Rusudan, and David VI Narin, son of Giorgi IV Lasha, as joint kings; they ruled the kingdom divided between the east, from Tbilisi, and the west, from Kutaisi, under Mongol overlordship, paid tribute and sent troops to the Ilkhanate's wars. David Ulu died in 1270.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Chronicle of a Hundred Years); Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

nodes.label: Demetre II
nodes.full: Demetre II, son of David Ulu, ruled east Georgia under the Ilkhans Abaqa and Arghun, and was executed by Arghun in 1289 after he was accused of complicity in a plot; the Georgian Church honoured him as a martyr, 'the self-sacrificer' (Tavdadebuli), because he is said to have gone to his death to spare the nobles of reprisal.
nodes.src: Chronicle of a Hundred Years; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Giorgi V
nodes.full: Giorgi V (Brtskinvale), king of Georgia from 1314, took advantage of the decline of the Ilkhanate after 1335 to stop the payment of tribute, expel the Mongol officials, reunite Imereti with the kingdom and restore royal authority over Samtskhe and the nobles; his rule is remembered as a second, short renaissance. He died in 1346, shortly before the plague.
nodes.src: Chronicle of a Hundred Years; Rapp 2003; Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).

nodes.label: Giorgi VII
nodes.full: Giorgi VII, son of Bagrat V, ruled through the later campaigns of Timur, who invaded Georgia eight times between 1386 and 1403; the king repeatedly submitted to the conqueror and promised tribute and troops, and after Timur's death in 1405 he and his son Constantine I tried to rebuild the kingdom. The invasions devastated towns and monasteries.
nodes.src: Thomas of Metsoph, History of Tamerlane; Nizam al-Din Shami, Zafarname; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Alexander I
nodes.full: Alexander I restored order and the economy after the Timurid invasions, refounded the churches and monasteries, tried to resettle the lands, and fought the Turkmen of Qara Qoyunlu and the Shirvanshahs; he is the last king of Georgia of the united kingdom's age, until he abdicated in 1442 and died as a monk.
nodes.src: Toumanoff 1963; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Dissolution of Georgia
nodes.full: Under Giorgi VIII (1446–1465) and the civil wars of his successors, with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople (1453) cutting Georgia's routes to the west and the Turkmen raiding from the east, the kingdom split about 1490 into three kingdoms, Kartli, Imereti and Kakheti, and the principality of Samtskhe, separate Bagrationi branches that were to last until the nineteenth century.
nodes.src: Vakhushti, Description; Toumanoff 1963; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Armenian princes
nodes.full: Under the Mongols Armenian princes held lands as vassals: the heirs of the Zakarids in Shirak and Lori, whose power declined in the later thirteenth century, the Orbelians in Syunik, which they ruled from Noravank and Tatev with the support of the Ilkhans, and the princes of Khachen in Artsakh. Smbat Sparapet, brother of the king of Cilicia, travelled to Karakorum.
nodes.src: Stepanos Orbelian, History of the State of Sisakan; Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Robert Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

nodes.label: Ilkhanids
nodes.full: Hulagu and his heirs ruled from Maragha and Tabriz the Ilkhanate, whose territories included Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan; the Ilkhans spent winters on the Mughan and Arran pastures and summers at Ala Dagh, and Ghazan's reforms made the region the core of the state. Azerbaijan and Arran became the Ilkhanate's heartland.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-tawarikh; Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the West (2005); John Andrew Boyle (ed.), Cambridge History of Iran, vol. 5 (1968).

nodes.label: Jalayirids
nodes.full: After the death of the last Ilkhan in 1335, the Jalayirids, a Mongol family, ruled Azerbaijan, Arran and Iraq from Tabriz and Baghdad, under Sheikh Hasan, Uways and Sultan Ahmad, contending with the Muzaffarids, Timur and then the Turkmen, until they were extinguished in the 1430s. Their court was a centre of Persian painting and poetry.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953); Boyle 1968.

nodes.label: Turkmen confederations
nodes.full: The Qara Qoyunlu ('Black Sheep') Turkmen under Qara Yusuf and Jahan Shah ruled Azerbaijan, Arran and Armenia from Tabriz in the fifteenth century, and the Aq Qoyunlu ('White Sheep') under Uzun Hasan took over after 1467 and ruled from Tabriz to 1501. These Turkmen furthered the Turkicisation of Azerbaijan and Arran.
nodes.src: Minorsky, 'Jihan-shah Qara-Qoyunlu', BSOAS (1954); John Woods, The Aqquyunlu (1976).

nodes.label: Shirvanshahs
nodes.full: The Kasranid Shirvanshahs kept Shirvan through Mongol and Timurid overlordship, with Ibrahim I (1382–1417), who allied with Timur, and Khalilullah I (1417–1462) and Farrukh Yasar (1462–1500), who built the palace in Baku and exercised a considerable autonomy until the Safavids killed Farrukh Yasar and took Shirvan in 1500–1501.
nodes.src: Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958); Woods 1976.

nodes.label: Berke and Hulagu
nodes.full: A war broke out between the Ilkhanate of Hulagu and the Golden Horde of Berke over Azerbaijan and the Caucasus pastures: the Golden Horde crossed the Caucasus by Derbent in 1262 and was beaten in 1263 and 1265 on the Terek and the Kura, with ravaging of Shirvan and Georgia; the war set the border between the two khanates on the range for a century.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din; Jackson 2005; Boyle 1968.

nodes.label: Timur’s seven-year war
nodes.full: In 1386 Timur entered the Caucasus, took Tbilisi in November, captured King Bagrat V and forced his conversion to Islam, ravaged Armenia and Georgia in 1387–1388 and in 1394 again. The Armenian historian Thomas of Metsoph, writing in the 1400s, records the destruction of monasteries, towns and villages and the removal of captives.
nodes.src: Thomas of Metsoph, History of Tamerlane and His Successors; Nizam al-Din Shami; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Terek
nodes.full: Timur marched in 1395 through Derbent and defeated the khan of the Golden Horde, Tokhtamysh, on the Terek river, in a battle that broke the Horde's power in the Caucasus and in the south of Russia; it was the greatest battle fought across the range.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Din Shami; Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarname.

nodes.label: Later invasions
nodes.full: Timur invaded Georgia again in 1399, 1400 and 1403, conducting a holy war with the burning of churches and monasteries, and extorting from Giorgi VII a promise of tribute and military aid; Georgian contingents were among the vassal forces of his army at Ankara in 1402.
nodes.src: Yazdi, Zafarname; Thomas of Metsoph; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Otlukbeli
nodes.full: In 1473 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II defeated the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan at Otlukbeli, near Erzincan, ending his hope of an empire from Anatolia to Khorasan; Uzun Hasan was linked by marriage to the court of Trebizond. The defeat halted Turkmen expansion westward.
nodes.src: Woods 1976; Halil İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age (1973).

nodes.label: Ismail in Shirvan
nodes.full: Shah Ismail, the young Safavid sheikh, set out from Ardabil in 1500 against the Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar, who had killed his father Haydar in 1488, defeated the army at Gulistan fortress, killed Farrukh Yasar and took Shamakhi and Baku before winning Tabriz in 1501.
nodes.src: Minorsky 1958; Roger Savory, Iran under the Safavids (1980).

nodes.label: Census and tumens
nodes.full: Möngke's census of 1254 counted households and taxed them in a head tax (qubchur) and land tax (kharaj), and the Mongols divided Georgia and Armenia into eight tumens for tax and levies; the Georgian kings were obliged to supply troops and the burden of the tribute heavy, until relief under Ghazan.
nodes.src: Kirakos Gandzaketsi 21; Rashid al-Din; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Clergy tax exemption
nodes.full: The Mongol khans' charters (yarlighs) exempted the churches and clergy of the conquered lands from taxation and forced service, as in the Armenian Church and the Georgian, the Orbelian monasteries and others receiving written privileges; the arrangement was upset when Ghazan became Muslim in 1295.
nodes.src: Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Stepanos Orbelian; Jackson 2005.

nodes.label: Law of Giorgi V
nodes.full: The Dasturlamali, a collection of laws attributed to Giorgi V the Brilliant, sets out the rules of the court and the offices of the realm, the punishments for crimes and the rights of the Church, and adapts older Georgian law and Byzantine and Mongol practice. It is the best surviving statement of Georgian public law of the time.
nodes.src: Dasturlamali of Giorgi V (ed. Dolidze); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Ghazan’s conversion
nodes.full: Ghazan, the Ilkhan, declared himself a Muslim in 1295 and ordered, at the urging of his general Nawruz, the destruction of churches, temples and synagogues in his lands, among them churches in Armenia and Georgia; the persecution lasted a few years before moderation under Ghazan's reforms. The shift ended the Mongol favour to Christians.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din; Stepanos Orbelian; Jackson 2005.

nodes.label: Gladzor and Tatev
nodes.full: The universities of Gladzor, founded about 1280 by the scholar Nerses Mshetsi and flourishing under Esai Nchetsi and Orbelian patronage, and of Tatev, with the teachers Hovhan Vorotnetsi and Grigor Tatevatsi in the late fourteenth century, taught theology, philosophy, grammar, music and miniature painting, and are regarded as the Armenian equivalent of the western universities.
nodes.src: Gladzor colophons; Stepanos Orbelian; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Etchmiadzin
nodes.full: In 1441 a council of Armenian clergy and nobles at Etchmiadzin elected Kirakos Virapetsi catholicos and restored the see to the old cathedral of Gregory, from Sis in Cilicia where it had been since 1292; the see in Cilicia continued under its own catholicos. The act made Etchmiadzin again the centre of the Armenian Church in the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Thomas of Metsoph; Garsoïan in R. Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 1 (1997).

nodes.label: Unitors
nodes.full: The Dominican Bartholomew of Bologna founded in 1330 at Qrna in Armenia the Order of the United Brothers of St Gregory the Illuminator (Fratres Unitores), whose monks adopted the Dominican rule and tried to bring the Armenians into union with Rome; the Order was opposed by the Armenian clergy of Syunik and survived into the fifteenth century.
nodes.src: Papal bull of John XXII (1328–1330); Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Hurufis
nodes.full: The Hurufi teacher Fazlullah Astarabadi, who taught the mystical meaning of the letters and the divinity of man, was seized in Shirvan and executed in 1394 at the castle of Alinja by Miran Shah, son of Timur; his follower the poet Nasimi was skinned alive at Aleppo in 1417 (some sources say 1404). Hurufism spread in Shirvan, Azerbaijan and Anatolia and influenced later Alevi and Bektashi thought.
nodes.src: Fazlullah, Javidan-nama; Hans Ritter; Minorsky 1958.

nodes.label: Momik
nodes.full: Momik, a sculptor, painter and architect who died about 1333, built for the Orbelians the church of the Holy Mother of God at Noravank (1339), with its carved portals and figured khachkars, and the church of Areni (1321), and he illuminated manuscripts, among them a Gospel of 1302; he is the finest artist of late medieval Armenia.
nodes.src: Noravank and Areni inscriptions; Sirarpie Der Nersessian, Armenian Art (1977).

nodes.label: Manuscripts of Gladzor and Tatev
nodes.full: The scriptoria of Gladzor and Tatev produced a series of illuminated Gospels and books, with scenes of the Last Judgement and the life of Christ, and the work of masters such as Toros Taronatsi and Momik, a school of miniature painting which spread with the Armenian clergy.
nodes.src: Gladzor Gospel (Matenadaran); Der Nersessian 1977.

nodes.label: Shirvanshah palace
nodes.full: The palace ensemble of the Shirvanshahs at Baku, with the palace buildings, the divan-khana, the mausoleum, the mosque and the tomb of the dynasty built from 1411 to the late fifteenth century, in local limestone, is the main surviving court architecture of medieval Azerbaijan and is a UNESCO site (2000) with the old walled city.
nodes.src: Palace inscriptions; UNESCO World Heritage no. 958 (2000).

nodes.label: Svaneti
nodes.full: In the mountain valleys of Svaneti, apart from the lowland wars, Georgian painters and metalworkers made wall-paintings, icons and repoussé crosses and covers, for the church towers and chapels of Ushguli, Lagurka and Mestia; the collections preserve many works from the period, such as the Mestia museum's icons.
nodes.src: Mestia and Svaneti museum collections; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Kirakos
nodes.full: Kirakos Gandzaketsi, a monk who had been a prisoner of the Mongols and learned their language, wrote at Khoranashat and Getik a History of Armenia from the fourth century to 1265, which is the main account of the Mongol conquest and Armenian life under the Ilkhans, and of the Zakarids, written by a witness.
nodes.src: Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History of the Armenians (trans. R. Bedrosian, 1986).

nodes.label: Vardan and Orbelian
nodes.full: Vardan Areveltsi (c. 1200–1271), who visited the Ilkhan Hulagu and the Cilician king, wrote a Universal History to 1267; the archbishop Stepanos Orbelian (c. 1250–1304) wrote the History of the State of Sisakan (Syunik), recording the Orbelian house and the monasteries with documents and inscriptions. They are the principal Armenian historians of the Mongol period.
nodes.src: Vardan Areveltsi, Historical Compilation (R. Thomson, Dumbarton Oaks Papers 43, 1989); Stepanos Orbelian, History of the State of Sisakan (trans. Brosset, 1864).

nodes.label: Thomas of Metsoph
nodes.full: Thomas of Metsoph, a monk and priest of Metsoph, wrote the History of Tamerlane and His Successors, a record of the Timurid invasions and of Turkmen rule in Armenia until 1446, with the tragedies of the villages and the disasters of the church, composed from eyewitnesses.
nodes.src: Thomas of Metsoph, History of Tamerlane and His Successors (trans. R. Bedrosian, 1987).

nodes.label: Frik
nodes.full: The poet Frik, a layman of the thirteenth century whose name means 'the unclean', wrote in the vernacular of the poor's wrongs under the Mongol-age nobility and clergy, in verse such as 'The Complaint' (Vaikh), and is a source of social protest in medieval Armenian literature; his poetry is humorous, bitter and unpolished.
nodes.src: Frik, Poems (ed. Ter-Grigorian); Der Nersessian 1977.

nodes.label: Nasimi
nodes.full: Imadaddin Nasimi, a poet of Shirvan born about 1369, wrote in Azerbaijani Turkic, Persian and Arabic the Hurufi doctrine that God's name is in man's face, and was executed in Aleppo in 1417; the Azerbaijanis revere him as a foundation of their literature in the vernacular.
nodes.src: Nasimi, Divan; Minorsky, 'Nasimi' in Encyclopaedia of Islam.

nodes.label: Chronicle of a Hundred Years
nodes.full: An anonymous Georgian chronicle, the Zhamtaaghmtsereli ('Chronicle of a Hundred Years'), written about 1363, tells the history of the Georgian kingdom from the death of Tamar (1213) to the years after 1318 and is the chief source for the Mongol period in Georgia.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba, Chronicle of a Hundred Years; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Tabriz–Trebizond road
nodes.full: Under the Mongol peace the roads from Tabriz through Armenia and Erzurum to Trebizond carried the trade of Persia and the East to the Black Sea, and the Italian cities, Genoa and Venice, set up consulates and colonies in Tabriz and on the Black Sea coast; Georgian lands lay on the northern branches of the same trade.
nodes.src: Marco Polo; Pegolotti, La pratica della mercatura; Jackson 2005.

nodes.label: Genoese slave trade
nodes.full: Italian merchants bought from Mongol slave dealers and from Caucasian chieftains many thousands of slaves from the Caucasus, among them Circassians, Georgians, Armenians and Mingrelians, and sold them in Egypt, Italy and Crete; the Genoese held trading stations on the Georgian coast at Sebastopolis (Sukhumi) and Phasis (Poti).
nodes.src: Charles Verlinden, L'esclavage dans l'Europe médiévale (1955); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Ghazan’s reforms
nodes.full: The Ilkhan Ghazan and his vizier Rashid al-Din reformed the tax system, replacing arbitrary levies with a fixed assessment, established controls on tax-farmers, encouraged the repair of irrigation canals and the settlement of nomads and tried to restore the land under cultivation in Azerbaijan and Arran. The measures eased the burden, for a time.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din, Tarikh-i Ghazani; Boyle 1968.

nodes.label: Canals and caravanserais
nodes.full: The Ilkhans and their successors repaired and built irrigation canals on the Araxes and Kura plains, with stations and caravanserais at intervals along the roads, among them those between Tabriz and the Black Sea, and the walls and bridges of the towns; some of the works lasted until the nineteenth century.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din; Minorsky 1958.

nodes.label: Envoys at Karakorum
nodes.full: In 1246–1250 the Georgian prince David Ulu, the Armenian constable Smbat Sparapet and, in 1254, King Hethum I of Cilicia journeyed to the great khan's court, seeking confirmation of their rule and alliance against the Muslims; the Armenian and Georgian accounts of the journeys are among the first descriptions of Mongolia.
nodes.src: Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Smbat Sparapet, Chronicle; Hethum of Korykos, Flor des estoires (c. 1307).

nodes.label: Clavijo
nodes.full: The Castilian ambassador Ruy González de Clavijo, sent by Henry III of Castile to Timur, crossed the Black Sea to Trebizond and travelled through Erzurum and Armenia to Tabriz and Samarkand in 1403–1406; his journal gives a picture of Armenia and Georgia, devastated by the Timurid wars.
nodes.src: Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane (trans. G. Le Strange, 1928).

nodes.label: Armenian dispersion
nodes.full: In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, fleeing the Mongols and Timur, many thousands of Armenians moved to the Crimea (Caffa), Moldavia, Poland and Russia, forming trading colonies in Lwów and Kamianets, and others went to Persia and Cyprus; the diaspora and its merchants became a new feature of Armenian life.
nodes.src: Garsoïan 1997; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Black Death
nodes.full: The plague of 1346–1348, which came from the steppe through the Genoese port of Caffa, reached the Georgian and Armenian lands and Azerbaijan, with recurring outbreaks; the Georgian chroniclers record a great mortality and its social disruption, and the plague contributed to the end of Giorgi V's revival.
nodes.src: Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Fall of Constantinople and Trebizond
nodes.full: The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 and Trebizond in 1461 left the Georgian kingdoms cut off from the Christian world and facing a Muslim ring of Turkmen and Ottoman states; their embassies to the West in the following decades sought help for a crusade.
nodes.src: Rapp 2003; İnalcık 1973.

nodes.label: Doquz Khatun
nodes.full: Doquz Khatun, the principal wife of Hulagu, a Nestorian Christian, protected the Christians of Persia, Georgia and Armenia in the early Ilkhanate, according to Armenian and Syriac sources, and interceded to save Baghdad's Christians in 1258; her death in 1265 was marked by the Christian communities.
nodes.src: Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Bar Hebraeus, Chronography; Jackson 2005.

nodes.label: Slaves of Caffa
nodes.full: Notarial acts from Genoese Caffa and Venice record the sale of slaves, with name, age, origin and price, among them girls and youths 'of Zichia', 'of the Mingrelians' or 'of the Armenians'; the Caucasus was one of the main sources of slaves for the Italian cities, taken by raiders and sold by debtors' families.
nodes.src: Notarial acts of Caffa (Bratianu); Verlinden 1955.

nodes.label: Craftsmen of Samarkand
nodes.full: After his campaigns Timur had large numbers of craftsmen, architects and artists carried off from the conquered towns, among them those of Tbilisi, Tabriz and Armenia, to build and adorn his capital of Samarkand, as Clavijo and the Persian chronicles record; the deportees seldom saw their homes again.
nodes.src: Clavijo; Yazdi, Zafarname; Thomas of Metsoph.

nodes.label: Köse Dağ and the Mongol conquest
nodes.full: In 1236–1243 the Mongol general Chormaghan conquered Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, and the victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 completed the subjugation of the highlands to the Ilkhanate.
nodes.src: background — see the Seljuks and the Georgian Golden Age folio (caucasus-1064-1243)
